https://www.crash.net/f1/news/1101936/1/.text: Carlos Sainz, Williams Racing, 2026 Hungary GP © XPB Images Prefer Crash.Net on Google See our stories more often Add Carlos Sainz says it was “impossible to avoid” hitting Oscar Piastri during the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix as he “has no idea I was about to get lapped. Following his pit stop from the lead of Sunday’s race at the Hungaroring, Oscar Piastri found himself mired in traffic. On lap 39 of 70, Piastri made contact with the Williams of Carlos Sainz exiting Turn 2, as the latter ran wide battling Aston Martin’s Fernando Alonso. Show X Embedded Content Loading this video will expose you to potential cookies and tracking by the provider It emerged after the race that there was an issue with the FIA’s blue flag system, with Sainz noting that he wasn’t aware he was about to be lapped. “At this stage I had no idea I was about to get lapped,” he told the media after finishing two laps down in 18th. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “On top of that, I was in a big fight with Fernando, trying to undercut him into the corner, and I would have expected Oscar to have been there. “And even if he was there, or where I would have expected, he was in my [blind] spot on the angle. “So, it was impossible from my side to avoid him. Read Also Alex Albon offers grim Williams outlook as James Vowles issues defiant message Williams’ 2026 F1 plight “an eye-opener” after it “overachieved” in 2025 “Probably a bit better communication would have helped, but at the same time it was a racing thing.” Sainz has “a pretty good excuse” why he shouldn’t have been penalised Sainz believes the issue with the blue flags should have led the stewards to declare the clash between himself and Piastri as a racing incident. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT He also suggests Piastri - who later dropped out with an unrelated gearbox failure - could have acted more cautiously at that point given the blue flag problems. Piastri and Sainz, seconds before making contact, at the Hungarian GP © XPB Images “To be honest, I’m really sorry for Oscar, but this time I think I have a pretty good excuse as to what happened,” he added. “I don’t know if he could also have been a bit more careful given he is the one fighting for a podium, and positioned himself a bit more cautiously, because of the issues we were all having with the blue flags. “But, OK, I took the five seconds, but I don’t care when I’m fighting for P18. It is what it is.” Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Sainz then said: “It’s a racing incident; he probably understands by knowing what happened. “He didn’t retire due to me or my fault. It was just a contact, and I’m glad it didn’t disturb his race too much. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r.text: Image source, AFP Image caption, Yemen's government says it has launched an offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis By David Gritten ,Â Helen Sullivan ,Â BBC News Â and Â Ottilie Mitchell ,Â BBC News Published 5 October 2026 Updated 15 minutes ago Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes. But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts. The Houthis said they had struck Riyadh's international airport on Monday, but have not commented regarding Mokha. Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating. Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area". Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town. Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab. The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive. Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia in an invocation of their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry. Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences". The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations". UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP. On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia". It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded. The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory. In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram. According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east. A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/14/turk.text: Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV news channel, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early on Wednesday."Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote in a post on X shortly before 7:00 am (0600 CET).Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda."In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility and the last was still being sought, it said.Mahiroğlu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.'We're under a blockade'In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building."The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That’s the situation...There’s nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague."At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can’t get into the institution where I’ve worked for 5 years, none of us can. The police haven’t left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu and some 400 other defendants.The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today...We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.And opposition leader Özgür Özel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly.""Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in İmamoğlu's trial."They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey’s biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"Last year, Halk TV, which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator, was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
